prompt: Many countries spend large amounts of public money on hosting international sporting events. Some people believe that this money is wasted. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
The complaint about hosting costs is usually aimed at the wrong target. Very little of the money goes on the sport. It goes on concrete, and it is the concrete that decides whether the spending was worth anything. I agree that most host nations waste public money, but the waste is a choice they make rather than a condition of hosting.

Consider what survives. A metro extension dug to move crowds to a stadium keeps moving commuters for fifty years; a flood-defence scheme built for a riverside venue protects the district long after the flags come down. Set against that is the athletics stadium, sized for one fortnight, unusable at that size afterwards, and expensive to keep standing while a city argues about what to do with it. Both come out of the same budget and are defended in the same speeches, but only one of them is an investment. The other is a monument, and monuments are what bids are actually won with.

The reason the second kind keeps being built is that the incentives reward it. Bids are judged on ambition, the officials who commit the money are usually gone before the maintenance bills arrive, and no politician has ever cut a ribbon on a hired venue. Cities that resisted this, reusing existing grounds and putting up temporary seating that came down again afterwards, have hosted perfectly good events for a fraction of the cost. That is the clearest evidence available that the expense is discretionary.

So the money is generally wasted, and it will go on being wasted while hosting is treated as an occasion for building rather than an occasion for organising. A country with something to gain should bid. It should simply decline to leave itself a stadium it cannot fill and a maintenance bill nobody voted for.
title: Whether hosting global sporting events wastes money
